title: Design a URL shortener
summary: The classic warm-up, done properly: requirements, estimates, base62 codes, counter ranges versus hashing, 301 versus 302, caching redirects and five years of storage.

steps.title: Requirements and estimates
body: **The ask:** turn `https://shop.example.com/sale/2026/winter?utm=mail` into `https://short.example.com/aZ3kQ9`, and send
anyone who opens the short link to the long one.
Ask before you draw. A good set of answers:
| Kind | Requirement |
| Functional | create a short link (optionally a custom alias and an expiry); redirect; count clicks |
| Non-functional | redirects are fast (p99 under 50 ms at the server) and very available (99.99%); codes are hard to guess |
| Out of scope | link previews, user accounts and billing, malware scanning (mention it, then park it) |
**Estimates** (say the arithmetic out loud):
```text
writes   100 M new links / month  = 100e6 / 2.6e6 s     ≈ 40 / s average
reads    100 reads per write                            ≈ 4,000 / s average
peak     about 3 x average                              ≈ 12,000 redirects / s
storage  100 M x 12 months x 5 years = 6 B links
6 B x ~500 bytes (URL, code, owner, dates, index) ≈ 3 TB, x 3 copies ≈ 9 TB
cache    80% of clicks hit ~20% of links: cache the hot set, tens of GB
The shape is clear before any box is drawn: **tiny writes, a huge read ratio, small rows**. This is a
read-path and caching problem, not a storage problem.

steps.prompt: A rival plan: 300 M new links a month, kept 3 years, about 400 bytes per link, before replication. Roughly how much storage?
steps.explain: 300 M x 36 months = 10.8 B links; x 400 bytes = 4.32 TB. Replication (x3) would make it about 13 TB. Still small enough that storage does not drive the design.

steps.title: API, data model and the high-level design
body: **API**
```text
POST /links            { "url": "https://...", "alias": "winter"?, "expiresAt": "..."? }
-> 201 { "code": "aZ3kQ9", "shortUrl": "https://short.example.com/aZ3kQ9" }
GET  /{code}           -> 302 Location: <long url>   (404 if unknown, 410 if expired)
GET  /links/{code}/stats -> { "clicks": 1234, ... }   (read from the analytics store, not the hot path)
**Data model.** One table keyed by `code`: `code (PK) | long_url | owner_id | created_at | expires_at`. Every
redirect is a point read by primary key, which any database does well. A key-value store fits too.
```text
browser -->|  CDN  |---->| load balancer |---->| redirect servers |---->| cache (hot) |
|          |               | miss
|          v               v
|   click events     +-----------+
|   -> stream ->     | links DB  |
v
id ranges from a counter service
Clicks are counted **off the hot path**: the redirect server publishes an event and returns at once. Writing
a counter row per click would turn 12,000 reads a second into 12,000 writes a second.

steps.prompt: Which redirect status gives each behaviour?
items: Browsers may cache it and skip the shortener next time
Every click reaches your servers, so it can be counted
Safe when the owner may change the target later
Search engines treat it as a permanent move
steps.explain: A 301 can be cached by browsers indefinitely, so you lose clicks and cannot change the target. Most shorteners answer 302 (or 307) and let the CDN cache it briefly with `Cache-Control: max-age`, which caps the load and keeps analytics.

steps.title: Where do codes come from?
body: A code is a number written in **base62** (`0-9`, `a-z`, `A-Z`). Seven characters give 62^7 = **3.5 trillion**
codes, about 590 times the 6 B links we need.
| Approach | How | Cost |
| Hash the URL | first 7 characters of base62(SHA-256(url)) | collisions: you must check the DB and retry on a clash; the same URL always gets the same code (good or bad) |
| One global counter | `INCR` on one row or key | a single hot spot and a single point of failure; codes are sequential and guessable |
| **Counter ranges** | each server leases a block of, say, 1,000 numbers and hands them out from memory | one coordination call per 1,000 links; a crash loses the rest of its block (gaps are fine) |
Ranges are the usual answer. To make codes **hard to guess**, do not hand them out in order: run the number
through a reversible shuffle (a keyed permutation of the 64-bit space) before base62, or keep the keyspace sparse
(use far fewer codes than exist). Sequential codes let anyone enumerate every link, including private ones.

steps.explain: 4000 = 1 x 62^2 + 2 x 62 + 32. Digit 32 is `w` (a is 10, so w is 10 + 22). Base62 is ordinary positional notation, written most significant digit first.

steps.prompt: Put the redirect path in order for a link that is not in the CDN yet.
lines: The browser resolves short.example.com and connects to the nearest CDN edge
The edge has no cached answer for GET /aZ3kQ9 and forwards it to the load balancer
A redirect server looks up aZ3kQ9 in the cache, and in the links DB on a miss
It publishes a click event to the stream without waiting, and answers 302 with the long URL
The edge keeps the 302 for its max-age, so the next clicks from that region stop at the edge
steps.explain: Every layer you add in front of the database removes load from the one behind it. The cost: clicks served by the edge never reach your servers, so either accept counting from CDN logs or keep the edge max-age short.

prompt: **Symptom first.** A celebrity posts one short link. Your dashboard at 20:05:
```text
redirect p99            8 ms  ->  940 ms
cache node cache-3 CPU  31%   ->  100%     (cache-1, -2, -4 .. -6 around 30%)
links DB CPU            22%   ->  24%
top key on cache-3      link:aZ3kQ9   61% of all GETs
What is the cause and the best first fix?
options: A hot key: one link lives on one cache node. Cache it in-process on the redirect servers for a few seconds (a near cache) and let the CDN hold the 302
The cache cluster is too small: add six more nodes
The database is the bottleneck: add read replicas
The load balancer is unbalanced: switch to least connections
steps.explain: All requests for one key go to the node that owns it, so more nodes do nothing for that key. A near cache (even a 1-second TTL) turns tens of thousands of cache calls into one per server per second. The DB is fine: the cache still answers, just slowly.

steps.title: Base62 codes
prompt: Write the two functions every shortener has:
- `string Encode(long n)`: `n` in base62 with the alphabet `0-9`, then `a-z`, then `A-Z`. `Encode(0)` is `"0"`.
A negative `n` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `long Decode(string code)`: the reverse. An empty code, or any character outside the alphabet, throws
`ArgumentException`.
`Encode(62)` is `"10"`, `Encode(4000)` is `"12w"` and `Decode("ZZ")` is `3843`.
solution: if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(code)) throw new ArgumentException("empty code", nameof(code));
if (d < 0) throw new ArgumentException($"'{c}' is not a base62 character", nameof(code));
hints: Encode: take `n % 62` as the last digit, then divide by 62, until `n` is 0. Build the string from the right.
Decode: start at 0 and for each character do `n = n * 62 + A.IndexOf(c)`.
template: Dojo.Eq("Encode(61) is the last digit", "Z", Encode(61));
Dojo.Eq("62^7 - 1 is the largest 7-character code", "ZZZZZZZ", Encode(3_521_614_606_207));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("Decode rejects an empty code", () => Decode(""));

steps.title: Bottlenecks and trade-offs, out loud
body: Close the design by naming what breaks first and what you chose:
- **Hot links** break first: one key, one cache node. Near cache plus a short CDN max-age.
- **302 over 301**: costs a request per click, buys analytics and editable targets.
- **Counter ranges over hashing**: no collision checks on write; codes need a shuffle so they are not guessable.
- **Clicks through a stream**: the stats are seconds behind, and the redirect never waits for them.
- **Storage is not the problem**: 9 TB fits one database cluster; shard by `code` later if writes grow.
- **Expiry**: check `expires_at` on read (410), and delete in a background job, not on the hot path.
Now build the range allocator that hands out the numbers.

steps.title: Counter ranges
prompt: Write a class `RangeAllocator` that hands out unique ids to many servers, with one shared counter call per block:
- `RangeAllocator(int blockSize)`: a block size of `0` or less throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `long Next(string server)`: the next id for that server. A server without a block, or whose block is used up,
leases the next block from the shared counter: blocks are `[0, blockSize)`, `[blockSize, 2 x blockSize)` and
so on, in the order they are leased.
- `int BlocksLeased`: how many blocks have been leased (the number of calls to the shared counter).
- `void Crash(string server)`: the server forgets its block. Its unused ids are lost for good (gaps are fine).
With a block size of 3: `Next("a")` is 0, `Next("b")` is 3, then `Next("a")` gives 1, 2, then 6.
solution: readonly Dictionary<string, (long Next, long End)> leases = new();
public int BlocksLeased { get; private set; }
if (!leases.TryGetValue(server, out var lease) || lease.Next == lease.End)
hints: Keep, per server, the next id to hand out and the end of its block: `Dictionary<string, (long Next, long End)>`.
When a server has no block or `Next == End`, lease `[nextBlockStart, nextBlockStart + blockSize)` and move `nextBlockStart` on.
template: Dojo.Eq("a gets the first block", 0L, dojoR.Next("a"));
Dojo.Eq("b gets the second block", 3L, dojoR.Next("b"));
Dojo.Eq("a carries on from memory", 1L, dojoR.Next("a"));
Dojo.Eq("a uses its last id", 2L, dojoR.Next("a"));
Dojo.Eq("a leases a new block when its own runs out", 6L, dojoR.Next("a"));
Dojo.Eq("after a crash b starts a fresh block (4 and 5 are lost)", 9L, dojoR.Next("b"));
Dojo.Eq("2,500 ids cost only 3 counter calls", 3, dojoBig.BlocksLeased);
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("block size must be positive", () => new RangeAllocator(0));

steps.title: Build it: cache the read path
prompt: A shortener is a read-heavy, skewed workload, exactly like the catalogue in this challenge. In the **System design
board**, put a cache cluster in front of the database, size it for the hot set, and run the load test until the
database utilisation and p99 goals are met within the budget.
steps.explain: Skew is what makes caching cheap: a cache that holds a small share of the keys can answer most of the reads. Size it for the hot set, not the whole data set.
